a: my son Methuselah
p: Chapters 91–108 are set as Enoch's farewell: a dying father teaching his family before he leaves.
b: The Epistle opens like a deathbed scene. Jacob gathers his sons in Genesis 49, Moses blesses the tribes in Deuteronomy 33, and later Jewish books such as the Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs are built entirely this way. A farewell speech lets an ancient hero speak to a much later audience: Enoch speaks to "the generations to come" (92:1). Methuselah's name is Matusala in Ge'ez; he is Enoch's son in Genesis 5:21. The other parts of 1 Enoch also use him as the one who receives and passes on his father's books (see 82:1 and 83:1).

a: a spirit has been poured out on me
p: Enoch speaks as a prophet: the spirit is poured out on him, as Joel promised for all God's people.
b: The Ge'ez says simply "a spirit" (mänfäs), with no article. Readers have taken it as God's Spirit or as a spirit of prophecy. The picture of a spirit "poured out" is from the prophets (Isaiah 32:15; Isaiah 44:3; Ezekiel 39:29; Joel 2:28). Peter quotes Joel's promise at Pentecost (Acts 2:17). Here the pouring marks Enoch as one who speaks for God before he speaks a word.
orig: መንፈስ ተክዕወ (mänfäs täkʿəwä), 'a spirit was poured out'

a: Enoch spoke to all his children about righteousness
p: Both Ge'ez texts say 'his children'; righteousness is what Enoch spoke. Charles's 'children of righteousness' is from other copies.
b: Dillmann prints wəludu ṣədqä: "his children" and then "righteousness" in the object form, the thing Enoch spoke about. The Ethiopian Church's printed text also has wəludu, "his children," but writes ṣədq without the object ending, which leaves the grammar loose. R. H. Charles translated "the children of righteousness," a phrase the book uses for the faithful (93:2; 105:2); that comes from Ethiopic manuscripts he followed, which this site has not identified, not from either printed text here. The Plain English Translation follows the two printed texts.
orig: ውሉዱ ጽድቀ (wəludu ṣədqä); EOTC ውሉዱ ጽድቅ (wəludu ṣədq)

a: walk in it
p: To 'walk' in Hebrew and Ge'ez means to live a certain way. The Epistle keeps the picture on purpose.
b: The Plain English Translation keeps the word "walk" (ḥorä) because the whole Epistle is built on it: two kinds of paths, walking in one or the other, and where each path ends (91:18–19; 94:1–4). In Hebrew halakh "walk" is the usual way to say "live," and later Jewish law is called halakhah, "the way you walk." Enoch himself "walked with God" (Genesis 5:24), so his teaching is about walking.

a: with a double heart
p: The Ge'ez says 'with two hearts': being two-faced or divided in loyalty, as in Psalm 12:2 and James.
b: The Ge'ez writes the numeral: "with 2 heart." The EOTC text spells it out, bä-kəlʾe ləb, "with two hearts." Psalm 12:2 has the same idea in Hebrew (lev valev, "heart and heart"), and Psalm 86:11 asks for a heart that is one. James calls the wavering person dipsychos, "two-souled" (James 1:8; James 4:8). To come to uprightness with a double heart is to want both paths at once.

a: violence will grow strong on the earth
p: The first punishment is the Flood: Genesis 6 says the earth was 'filled with violence.'
b: Verses 5–10 tell history twice. First violence grows and a great punishment comes (the Flood); then injustice grows again "a second time" (91:6) and a final judgment comes (91:7–9). The pattern follows Genesis 6:11–13, where the earth is "filled with violence" before the Flood. The Ge'ez word gəfʿ means violence or oppression; in the woes it becomes the oppression of the poor by the rich.

a: a second time
t: Two judgments: the Flood and the end
p: Enoch sees the Flood as a pattern for the last judgment. Jesus and 2 Peter use the same pattern.
b: Many Jewish writings of this period treat the Flood as the first world judgment and a preview of the last one (10:2–22; 93:4). Jesus compares the coming of the Son of Man to the days of Noah (Matthew 24:37–39). 2 Peter 3:5–7 sets the world once destroyed by water beside the world kept for fire. Ethiopian Orthodox teachers read verses 5–9 as Enoch's true prophecy of both. Most scholars read the second judgment as the writer's own hope for his time.

a: The holy Lord will come out
p: God 'coming out' of his place to judge is a picture from the prophets and from the opening of 1 Enoch.
b: Micah 1:3 and Isaiah 26:21 say the LORD is "coming out of his place" to punish the earth. The same scene opens 1 Enoch, where the Holy Great One comes out from his dwelling and treads on Mount Sinai (1:3–4, 9). Jude 14–15 quotes that opening. The Epistle returns to the picture so that its warnings sit inside the same story.

a: their towers will burn with fire
p: The Ge'ez word means 'tower.' Charles turned it into 'temples' and added 'idols' to the verse.
b: The Ge'ez says "everything will be handed over with the nations," then maḫfäd, "tower," burns. R. H. Charles (1912) changed the line to "all the idols of the heathen will be abandoned, and the temples burned," which reads well but is a guess. A tower may stand for the fortified power of the nations, or for a temple-tower. Either way the verse sees the end of pagan rule and pagan worship, as Zephaniah 2:11 and Zechariah 13:2 do.

a: The righteous will rise from their sleep
p: Is this the resurrection of the dead, or the waking of the faithful to wisdom? Readers differ.
b: "Sleep" is a common word for death (Daniel 12:2; 1 Thessalonians 4:13), and 92:3 repeats the line. Many scholars hear a resurrection here, one of the earliest in Jewish writing, older than Daniel 12:2 or close to it. Others read it as the faithful waking up spiritually, since the next line says "wisdom will rise" with them. Ethiopian Orthodox and most Christian readers take it as resurrection, as Paul uses "those who have fallen asleep" (1 Corinthians 15:20).

a: After that the roots of injustice will be cut off
t: Why the weeks are out of order
p: Verses 91:11–17 finish the 'Ten Weeks' that start in 93:1–10. The Aramaic scroll 4Q212 shows the original order.
b: In every Ethiopic manuscript, weeks eight to ten (91:12–17) come before weeks one to seven (93:3–10). The Aramaic copy from Qumran, 4Q212 (4QEnoch-g, copied in the first century BC), puts 93:9–10 right before 91:11–17, as J. T. Milik published it (1976). So the Ten Weeks once ran in order: 93:1–10, then 91:11–17. Somewhere in the Greek or Ethiopic copying the page was moved. This site keeps Charles's verse numbers, so read 93:1–10 first, then come back here.

a: The blasphemers will be cut off in every place
p: Dillmann's Ge'ez here is hard to read. The EOTC text and most translators read 'blasphemers.'
b: Dillmann prints a word (ʾəm-ṣəfufan) that does not give clear sense, and Charles left a gap in his English. The Ethiopian Church's printed text reads wä-ʾəmənä ḍərufan, "and from the blasphemers," which fits the end of the verse. In the Aramaic order this verse ends the seventh week: the chosen ones of 93:10 are sent to uproot violence and deceit. See the variant.
orig: ወእምነ ፡ ፅሩፋን (wä-ʾəmənä ḍərufan), 'and from the blasphemers'

a: the week of righteousness
p: The 'weeks' are ages of world history, ten in all, each probably seven units long.
b: Daniel 9:24–27 counts "seventy weeks" (seventy sevens) to the end; here all of history is ten weeks. Seven is the number of completeness, and ten weeks of seven make seventy, the number of Jeremiah's exile (Jeremiah 25:11). The writer places himself at the end of the seventh week (93:9–10), so the eighth, ninth and tenth are still to come for him: a time of the righteous sword, a judgment on the whole world, and judgment on the Watchers.

a: A sword will be given to it
p: The righteous are handed a sword. Is this a call to arms, or God's own judgment?
b: Some scholars connect the sword with the Maccabean revolt against Antiochus IV (167–164 BC), and read the line as support for armed resistance (compare 90:19 in the Dream Visions). Others note that the text says nothing of fighting: judgment is given to the righteous, as in Daniel 7:22 and Wisdom of Solomon 3:8. Christian readers have heard echoes of the saints judging the world (1 Corinthians 6:2; Revelation 20:4). The Plain English Translation keeps "a sword will be given" without deciding.

a: a house will be built for the Great King
t: A house for the Great King
p: A new temple at the end of history. Readers ask which temple, built by whom.
b: "House" means temple in the Apocalypse of Weeks (93:7–8). The Great King is God (Psalm 48:2; Malachi 1:14; Matthew 5:35). Jewish readers of the 100s BC hoped for a pure new temple, as in 90:28–29 and the Temple Scroll from Qumran. Christian readers connect it with the church as God's house (1 Peter 2:5) or the New Jerusalem, where John sees no temple because God is its temple (Revelation 21:22).

a: The world will be written down for destruction
p: The Ge'ez has the world 'written down' for destruction. The Aramaic, as Milik restores it, throws wicked works into the Pit.
b: Heavenly books are everywhere in this part (98:7–8; 103:2; 104:7; 108:3), and the Ge'ez here has the whole world, not just sinners, "written down" for an end. The Aramaic copy 4Q212 is damaged at this point but keeps more than a few letters, and it says something different. As J. T. Milik restores it (1976, p. 281), righteous judgment is revealed "for all the children of the whole earth," and the works of the wicked are "cast into the [eternal] Pit" (the bracket marks his restoration). Milik also notes that a Greek translator rendered "the Pit" as "perdition" (p. 283), which may be how "destruction" came into the Ethiopic; that link is a suggestion. See the variant. The last line, that all people will look to the path of uprightness, echoes the promise that all nations will stream to God's teaching (Isaiah 2:2–3).

a: It will be carried out on the Watchers
p: The Ge'ez is tangled here. Most read: the last judgment falls on the Watchers, the angels who sinned.
b: Word for word the Ge'ez says the judgment "will be done from the Watchers, and the great eternal heaven that will spring up from among the angels." Charles rewrote it as "vengeance amongst the angels." The Aramaic of 4Q212 is damaged here. As J. T. Milik restores it (1976, p. 281), the tenth week brings "an eternal Judgement" and "the (fixed) time of the Great Judgement," and elsewhere he describes this verse as the final judgment on "the watchers of heaven" (p. 66). All agree on the main point: the story that began with the Watchers' sin (6:1–8; 10:12) ends with their judgment. The Watchers' name, təguhan, is explained at 1:5.

a: a new heaven will appear
t: A new heaven: Compared with the Bible
p: Agrees with Isaiah, 2 Peter and Revelation that the present heavens pass away and new ones come.
b: This matches the 66 books closely. Isaiah 65:17 and 66:22 promise "new heavens and a new earth"; 2 Peter 3:13 and Revelation 21:1 repeat it. Enoch speaks only of a new heaven here, perhaps because his Watchers sinned in heaven and the stars went astray (18:15). Revelation's "the first heaven ... had gone away" (Revelation 21:1) is very close to this verse. Most scholars think Isaiah is the common source, not that Revelation borrowed from Enoch.

a: seven times as bright
p: Isaiah 30:26 promises the sun will shine seven times brighter on the day God heals his people.
b: The image comes from Isaiah 30:26: "the sun's light will be seven times as strong." The Ge'ez writes the numeral seven. In the Astronomical Book the lights of heaven keep a fixed order (72–82); here at the end they are not destroyed but made brighter.

a: sin will never be mentioned again
p: Compare Isaiah 65:17: the former things will not be remembered or come to mind.
b: The tenth week does not end history; it opens onto "many weeks without number." The promise that sin will not even be named again echoes Isaiah 65:17 and Jeremiah 31:34 ("their sin I will remember no more"). Revelation 21:4 says the same of death and pain: "The first things have gone away."

a: the paths of righteousness and the paths of violence
p: Two paths, one to life and one to death: a teaching shared by Deuteronomy, Psalm 1, Jesus and the Didache.
b: Moses sets life and death before Israel (Deuteronomy 30:15–19). Psalm 1 contrasts the way of the righteous and the way of the wicked, and Jeremiah 21:8 offers "the way of life and the way of death." Jesus speaks of the wide and narrow roads (Matthew 7:13–14), and the early Christian Didache opens: "There are two ways." The Epistle of Enoch is one of the fullest Jewish examples from before Jesus.

a: Enoch the scribe
p: Scholars think the Epistle once began here. Its title, 'Epistle of Enoch,' survives in the Greek papyrus.
b: This verse reads like the heading of a book: who wrote it, what it is, and for whom. Many scholars think chapters 92–105 once circulated on their own, with 91 added as an introduction. The Greek Chester Beatty–Michigan papyrus ends its copy of these chapters with the title Epistle of Enoch (after 107:3), as Campbell Bonner published it (1937). Enoch is "the scribe" also in 12:4 and 15:1: the first person to learn writing.

a: praised by all people and judge of the whole earth
p: The Ge'ez says 'praised by all people, and judge of all the earth' without saying who. Most take these as Enoch's titles.
b: Word for word the Ge'ez runs "from all people praised, and judge of all the earth," with no word for "the one" and no clear subject. Most translators take the phrases as Enoch's titles: praised by all people, and a judge, because in other Enoch books he records the deeds of all people for the judgment (Jubilees 4:23; 2 Enoch). "Judge of all the earth" is God's title in Genesis 18:25, which is why some readers apply the words to the wisdom Enoch passes on instead. The Plain English Translation puts them after Enoch's name, the most common reading. The Aramaic 4Q212 keeps part of this verse with different titles: as Milik restores it (1976, p. 274), Enoch is "the scribe of distinction" and, in restored words, "the wisest of men."
orig: ስቡሕ ወመኰንነ ኵሉ ምድር (səbuḥ wä-mäkʷännə kʷəllu mədr)

a: the Holy Great One
p: A favorite name for God in 1 Enoch. Here the Ge'ez puts 'holy' first; at 97:6 it puts 'great' first.
b: Qədus ʿäbiy, "the Holy Great One," is how 1 Enoch most often names God (see 1:3). It combines Isaiah's "the Holy One of Israel" with the greatness of the heavenly King. This site renders it "the Holy Great One" in every part of 1 Enoch. The Epistle uses it at 92:2, 97:6, 98:6 and 104:9, along with "the Most High" (ləʿul) and "the Great One" (103:4; 104:1).

a: has set days for everything
p: Do not despair over evil times: God has already set the days. Compare Ecclesiastes 3 and Daniel.
b: Readers living through hard times are told that the calendar of history is fixed in heaven. Ecclesiastes 3:1 says there is "a time for everything," and Daniel's visions keep saying the end will come "at the appointed time" (Daniel 11:27, 35). Jesus says the Father has set the times by his own authority (Acts 1:7).

a: walk in light that lasts forever
p: The righteous walk in light; sin perishes in darkness (92:5). Light and darkness divide the two groups.
b: Light for the righteous and darkness for sinners runs through these chapters and ends the book (108:11–14). Isaiah 60:19–20 promises that the LORD will be an everlasting light. The Dead Sea Scrolls call the faithful "the sons of light," and the New Testament calls believers "children of light" (John 12:36; Ephesians 5:8; 1 Thessalonians 5:5).

a: the plant of righteousness
p: Israel as a plant God has set in the ground: here it grows from Abraham to the chosen ones of the writer's day.
b: The Hebrew prophets picture Israel as a vine or plant that God planted (Isaiah 5:7; Isaiah 60:21; Isaiah 61:3, "Oaks of Righteousness, the LORD's planting"). In the Ten Weeks, the plant starts with one man (93:5, probably Abraham), becomes a people, and ends as "the eternal plant of righteousness" from which a chosen group is picked (93:10). The Dead Sea Scrolls use the same picture for their own community (Damascus Document 1:7).

a: the heavenly tablets
p: Heaven keeps written tablets that record history before it happens. Jubilees and the Epistle both use them.
b: Enoch claims three sources: a vision, the words of angels, and the heavenly tablets. The tablets are a heavenly record of what God has decided, read by Enoch (81:1–2; 103:2; 106:19). The book of Jubilees uses "the heavenly tablets" over and over for laws and events. The Bible has heavenly books too: the book of life (Exodus 32:32; Psalm 139:16; Daniel 7:10; Revelation 3:5; Revelation 20:12).

a: I was born the seventh, in the first week
p: Enoch was the seventh generation from Adam (Genesis 5). Jude 14 calls him 'the seventh from Adam.'
b: Counting Adam, Seth, Enosh, Kenan, Mahalalel, Jared and Enoch gives seven (Genesis 5:3–18). Jude 14 calls Enoch "the seventh from Adam" just before quoting 1 Enoch 1:9, and 1 Enoch 60:8 has the same phrase. Because Enoch is seventh in the first week, each week may be seven generations long; that is one common way to count the weeks. The Aramaic 4Q212 preserves this verse, and a Coptic fragment of 93:3–8 is also reported; this part has not checked the Coptic.

a: a man will be saved
t: Week two: Noah and the Flood
p: The 'first end' is the Flood, and the man saved is Noah. The law for sinners may be God's covenant with Noah.
b: Each week is a short riddle. Week two: evil and deceit arise (the Watchers, 6:1–8:4), the first end comes (the Flood), and a man is saved (Noah, Genesis 6:8). After it, God makes "a law for the sinners": most read this as the rules given to Noah's descendants in Genesis 9:1–7, which later rabbis called the laws of the sons of Noah. Some read "he" as Noah, others as God.

a: a man will be chosen as the plant of righteous judgment
p: The chosen man is almost surely Abraham, and the plant that comes after him is Israel.
b: Abraham is the man God chose (Genesis 12:1–3; Nehemiah 9:7), and his descendants are the plant of righteousness. Isaiah 51:1–2 calls Abraham the rock from which Israel was cut. The Ten Weeks skip Isaac, Jacob and Joseph to move fast toward the writer's own day.

a: an enclosure
t: Week four: Sinai and an enclosure
p: Visions, a law for every generation, and an 'enclosure': Moses at Sinai, and perhaps the tabernacle's court.
b: Week four is Moses: the holy and righteous see visions (Exodus 24:9–11; the burning bush), and a law "for every generation" is given at Sinai. The Ge'ez ʿäṣäd means a fenced court. Scholars read it as the courtyard of the tabernacle (Exodus 27:9), as the land of Israel, or as the Law itself, which the Letter of Aristeas (139) describes as a fence around Israel. The Mishnah's "make a fence around the Torah" (Avot 1:1) is a different picture: rules that guard the Law.
r: Exodus 19:1–20:21; Exodus 27:9–18; Exodus 24:9–11; Letter of Aristeas 139

a: the house of glory and of the kingdom
p: The house of glory is the temple Solomon built, with the kingdom of David's family.
b: The house is the temple in Jerusalem (1 Kings 6–8), filled with God's glory (1 Kings 8:10–11), and "kingdom" points to David's dynasty. The writer says it will be built "forever," echoing God's promise to David (2 Samuel 7:13). The next week tells how that house burned.

a: a man will go up
t: Week six: Elijah, the fall of Jerusalem and exile
p: Blindness, a man taken up to heaven (Elijah), the temple burned (586 BC) and the people scattered.
b: Week six covers the kingdoms of Israel and Judah. People turn from wisdom, as the books of Kings tell. The man who "goes up" is Elijah, carried up in a whirlwind (2 Kings 2:11); like Enoch, he left the earth without dying. At the end of the week the house of the kingdom is burned, which happened when Babylon destroyed Jerusalem in 586 BC (2 Kings 25:9), and the chosen root is scattered into exile.

a: a perverse generation will arise
t: Week seven: the writer's own time
p: The seventh week runs from the exile to the writer's day: a crooked generation, in his eyes.
b: Nothing good is said of the return from exile or of the second temple. That is striking: Ezra and Nehemiah celebrate the rebuilding, but this writer calls the whole period "perverse" (compare 89:73, where the rebuilt temple's bread is called unclean). This fits a group that thought the temple leadership of its day had gone wrong. "Perverse generation" comes from Deuteronomy 32:5.

a: chosen righteous ones will be chosen
t: The chosen ones of the seventh week
p: The writer's own group: chosen from Israel's plant and given special wisdom. Who were they?
b: This is where the writer stands. A group is picked out of the "eternal plant" and given sevenfold teaching about creation, meaning the wisdom found in Enoch's books. In the Aramaic of 4Q212, as Milik and Nickelsburg read it, they are chosen "as witnesses of righteousness." Scholars link them to the circles that produced the Enoch books, possibly ancestors of the community at Qumran. Ethiopian Orthodox readers have taken the chosen ones as the faithful of every age, including the apostles and the church.

a: Is there any human being who can hear the voice of the Holy One and not be shaken?
p: These questions sound like God's questions to Job. The surprise is that Enoch can answer them.
b: Verses 11–14 pile up questions like those God asks Job (Job 38:4–5, 18, 31–33) and Isaiah 40:12: who has measured the earth and counted the stars? 4 Ezra 4:5–9 uses the same kind of list. The expected answer is "no one." But in 1 Enoch, Enoch has done exactly these things: angels took him to see the ends of the earth and the paths of the stars (chapters 17–36 and 72–82). The questions may set his revealed knowledge apart from all other human wisdom.

a: see all their ends
p: The Ge'ez word can mean 'ends, corners' or 'wings.'
b: ʾäknaf is the plural of kənf, which means both a wing and an edge or corner, like the Hebrew kanaf ("the four corners of the earth," Isaiah 11:12). Here it probably means the far ends of heaven. Some translators read the wings of the heavenly beings.

a: certain people of a generation to come
t: A chosen few in a later generation
p: Some people in a future generation will see the two paths clearly and turn from violence.
b: The Ge'ez is "known people from a generation." Most read this as the same group as the chosen ones of 93:10: Enoch foresees that in the writer's time some will understand his teaching. It is a way of telling the first readers that they are the ones Enoch had in mind.

a: a life worth choosing
p: The Ge'ez says 'choose ... a chosen life,' a play on words the Plain English Translation tries to keep.
b: "Choose" (ḫəryu) and "chosen" (ḫərit) come from the same root as ḫəruy, "chosen one," the title of the Chosen One in the Parables (see 39:6). The readers are "chosen" (93:10), and now they must choose. Deuteronomy 30:19 says the same: "choose life."

a: No place will be found for her
p: Wisdom finds no place among people, as in the Parables of Enoch and in Proverbs.
b: Wisdom is pictured as a woman, as in Proverbs 1:20–33 and 8:1–36. The Parables tell how Wisdom came to live among people, found no home, and went back to heaven (see 42:1–2). Sirach 24 tells the opposite story, in which Wisdom settles in Israel as the Law. John 1:10–11 uses a similar pattern for the Word.

a: Woe to those who build injustice and violence
t: The woes: a sermon for real people
p: About thirty woes fill chapters 94–100. They speak to poor, oppressed Jews about the rich who wrong them.
b: A "woe" is a cry of grief at someone's coming doom, used by the prophets against the rich and powerful (Isaiah 5:8–23; Amos 6:1; Habakkuk 2:6–19). The Epistle has about thirty of them in chapters 94–100, and two more at 103:5 and 103:8. Its targets are rich, powerful people who build fine houses, cheat in court, trust in wealth and persecute the righteous. The first hearers seem to have been poor or powerless Jews in Judea in the 100s BC. The woes speak to the sinners, but they are written for the righteous who hear the letter (compare 97:2), to comfort them. The sinners are quoted at times (97:8–9; 102:6–8; 103:5–6), but always so that Enoch can answer them.

a: Woe to those who build their houses with sin!
p: Jeremiah and Habakkuk condemn those who build houses with unjust profit.
b: The building image runs through the woes (94:6–7; 99:13). Jeremiah 22:13 cries woe to the one who builds his house without justice and makes his neighbor work for nothing. Habakkuk 2:9–12 cries woe to one who builds a town with blood. Jesus' story of the wise and foolish builders turns the same picture (Matthew 7:24–27).

a: Woe to you rich!
p: Luke 6:24 has Jesus say the same words. James 5:1–6 reads like a short version of these woes.
b: "Woe to you who are rich" (Luke 6:24) stands in Luke's Sermon on the Plain English Translation, which pairs blessings for the poor with woes for the rich, as the Epistle does. James 5:1–6 condemns the rich for hoarding, cheating workers and condemning the righteous. George Nickelsburg showed how close Luke's teaching on wealth is to these chapters. Most scholars see shared Jewish tradition, not direct copying.

a: you did not remember the Most High
p: Ləʿul, 'the Most High,' is the Epistle's most common name for God.
b: Ləʿul means "the one on high" and matches the Hebrew Elyon (Genesis 14:18; Psalm 91:1) and the Greek Hypsistos (Luke 1:32). Forgetting God in times of plenty is the warning of Deuteronomy 8:11–14, where wealth leads people to forget the LORD.

a: your Creator will rejoice when you are destroyed
t: God rejoicing at destruction: Compared with the Bible
p: Deuteronomy 28:63 says this too. Ezekiel 18:23 says God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked.
b: This goes along with one strand of the Bible and against another. Deuteronomy 28:63 says the LORD will "take delight" in destroying the disobedient, and Proverbs 1:26 has Wisdom laugh at the fool's disaster. But Ezekiel 18:23 and Ezekiel 33:11 say God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked, and 2 Peter 3:9 says he wants all to repent. Ethiopian Orthodox teachers read the verse as a warning of justice, not a denial of mercy. Readers from other churches test it by the whole Bible's teaching.

a: will be a reproach to the sinners
p: The righteous will either be mocked by sinners, or their lives will put the sinners to shame.
b: The Ge'ez ṣəʾlät means a reproach or insult. It may mean that sinners will mock the righteous in those days (compare 102:6–8), or that the righteous will stand as a rebuke to them. Wisdom of Solomon 5:1–5 imagines the wicked seeing the righteous they once mocked now counted among the children of God.

a: If only my eyes were a cloud full of water!
p: Enoch weeps over the sinners as Jeremiah wished his eyes were a fountain of tears.
b: The Ge'ez begins "Who will give me," a Hebrew way of saying "If only" (mi yitten). Jeremiah 9:1 (Hebrew 8:23) wishes his head were water and his eyes a fountain of tears, to weep for his people. Enoch the judge is also Enoch the mourner. Jesus weeps over Jerusalem (Luke 19:41).
orig: መኑ ይሁበኒ (männu yəhubäni), 'who will give me'

a: The Lord will once again hand them over to you
p: The Ge'ez here is ʾƎgziʾabḥer, the usual name for God in the Ethiopian Bible.
b: ʾƎgziʾabḥer means "Lord of the land" and is the Ge'ez Bible's word for God, standing where the Hebrew has the divine name YHWH. The Epistle also uses the shorter ʾƎgziʾ, "Lord" (91:7; 97:5). The Plain English Translation gives both as "the Lord." "Once again" may look back to victories such as the judges' or the Maccabees', when God handed enemies over to Israel.

a: who lay curses that cannot be lifted
p: Literally 'who bind bans so that they cannot be loosed.' Curses were real weapons in the ancient world.
b: The Ge'ez speaks of binding a ban (gəzätat) that cannot be untied. People in the ancient world wrote curse tablets and pronounced bans to harm enemies or force a court case. A ban could also mean being cut off from the community. "Binding and loosing" is the same language Jesus uses of the authority to forbid and permit (Matthew 16:19; Matthew 18:18).

a: You will be paid back for what you have done
p: Repaying people for their deeds is a refrain of the Epistle (95:5; 100:7), as in Psalm 62 and Romans 2.
b: The idea that God repays each person for what they have done is everywhere in the Bible: Psalm 62:12; Proverbs 24:12; Matthew 16:27; Romans 2:6; Revelation 22:12. Enoch adds that the payback mirrors the crime: those who repay evil are repaid, those who hunt are hunted (95:7).

a: you hunt down the righteous
p: The Epistle speaks of real persecution. Scholars debate whether it means Jews, foreign rulers, or both.
b: The sinners in the woes are mostly Jews: they break "the eternal law" (99:2), reject the inheritance of their fathers (99:14) and twist the words of uprightness. Some scholars think of Hellenizing aristocrats before the Maccabean revolt; others of Hasmonean rulers and their supporters around 100 BC, who were sometimes harsh to religious opponents. Ethiopian Orthodox readers apply the woes to oppressors in every age. The Bible's own portrait of persecution is similar (Psalm 37:12–14).

a: like rock badgers hiding from the unjust
p: Rock badgers (hyraxes) are small animals that hide in rocky cliffs. The righteous will be safe like them.
b: The rock hyrax, or rock badger, lives in cracks of cliffs in Israel and Ethiopia and dashes in at any danger. Psalm 104:18 and Proverbs 30:26 praise it for making its home in the rocks. The picture is of the faithful finding safety while the unjust fall. Eagles' nests above the vultures come from Obadiah 4 and Isaiah 40:31.

a: wail like sirens
p: The Ge'ez borrows the Greek word 'sirens.' The Greek Old Testament uses it for wailing desert creatures.
b: Ṣedenat is the Greek seirēnes, sirens, the singing creatures of Greek legend. The Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible already used "sirens" for wailing animals of the ruins, such as jackals and owls (Isaiah 13:21; Isaiah 34:13; Micah 1:8). The machine verse cut put these words in 96:3, but they finish the sentence of 96:2.

a: you will hear a voice of rest from heaven
p: Rest from heaven for those who suffered: compare Hebrews 4 and Revelation 14:13.
b: The suffering righteous are promised healing, light and a heavenly voice of rest. Revelation 14:13 has a voice from heaven say that those who die in the Lord "can rest from their hard work." Hebrews 4:9–11 speaks of a Sabbath rest that remains for God's people.

a: Your wealth makes you look like the righteous
t: Wealth as a sign of blessing: Compared with the Bible
p: Many thought wealth proved God's favor. Enoch denies it, as Job, the prophets and Jesus do.
b: Parts of the Bible link wealth with God's blessing (Deuteronomy 28:1–14; Proverbs 10:22). Enoch says the rich only look righteous. This agrees with Job's protest (Job 21:7–13), with Psalm 73, and with Jesus' warning that it is hard for the rich to enter the kingdom (Mark 10:23–25). It goes beyond the 66 books in how fully it sets "the rich" and "the sinners" side by side as one group.

a: drink the strength from the very root of the spring
p: The Ge'ez is odd: 'the strength of the root of the spring.' Charles changed it to 'wine in large bowls.'
b: Word for word the Ge'ez says "drink the strength of the root of the spring," probably the freshest water from the head of a spring, in a dry land where water was precious. Charles changed it to "wine in large bowls," after Amos 6:6 ("They drink wine by the bowlful"). The Plain English Translation keeps the Ge'ez. Either way the rich take the best for themselves and "trample the lowly" (Amos 2:7; Amos 4:1).

a: you have abandoned the spring of life
p: Jeremiah 2:13: God's people left him, 'the spring of living water.'
b: The verse plays on water: the rich drink water whenever they like, but they have left the true spring. Jeremiah 2:13 and Jeremiah 17:13 call the LORD "the spring of living water," and Psalm 36:9 says "with you is the spring of life." Jesus offers living water (John 4:10–14), and Revelation 21:6 promises water from the spring of life.

a: who use your might to crush the righteous
p: The 'mighty' are the powerful of society: landowners, officials, rulers.
b: Dillmann reads "you mighty ones"; the EOTC text reads "you sinners" (see the variant). The mighty use their might to crush the righteous, which fits the whole sermon: the conflict is between the powerful and the powerless. The Ge'ez verb kʷärʿä means to strike someone on the head. Compare Mary's song: "He has pulled rulers down from thrones / and raised the lowly high" (Luke 1:52).

a: the Most High has your destruction in mind
p: The 'you' suddenly changes from the righteous (97:1) to the sinners. Charles added 'ye sinners.'
b: Verse 1 speaks to the righteous; verse 2 turns to the sinners without saying so. Charles added "(ye sinners)" to make it clear. The Epistle often switches its audience like this, sometimes inside one verse (99:1–2). The sinners are spoken about for the sake of the righteous who hear the letter read.

a: the angels will rejoice over your destruction
t: Angels rejoicing: Compared with the Bible
p: The angels here rejoice at the sinners' end. Jesus says the angels rejoice when a sinner repents.
b: In Luke 15:7, 10 there is joy among the angels over one sinner who repents. In Revelation 18:20 and 19:1–3 heaven rejoices over Babylon's fall because justice has been done for the martyrs. The Epistle stands with Revelation: the angels are glad when oppression ends. It never speaks of the rich repenting, though 98:4 places the blame for sin on human choice.

a: when you hear the sound of the prayer of the righteous
p: The cries of the wronged reach God and set judgment in motion, as with Abel's blood and the martyrs under the altar.
b: Prayer in the Epistle is a legal act. The righteous are told to pray so the angels will bring their case before God (97:5; 99:3; 104:3). In Genesis 4:10 Abel's blood cries from the ground; in Exodus 3:7 God hears the Israelites' cry; in James 5:4 the cries of cheated harvesters reach the Lord of Armies; and in Revelation 6:9–10 the martyrs cry "How long?"
r: Genesis 4:10; Exodus 3:7; James 5:4; Revelation 6:9–10; Revelation 8:3–5; Luke 18:7

a: You kept company with sinners
p: The charge against them at the judgment: they kept company with sinners. In 104:6 the righteous are told not to.
b: The Ge'ez sutufan, "companions, partners," is the same word as in 104:6, where the righteous must not be companions of sinners but will be companions of the army of heaven. Psalm 1:1 blesses the one who does not sit with mockers. Dillmann's text reads "you will not be like them"; the EOTC text reads "but" and "against them."

a: Every word of your injustice will be read out
p: From 97:6 to 107:3 an older Greek copy survives, the Chester Beatty–Michigan papyrus of the 300s AD.
b: Most of the Epistle survives only in Ge'ez. But for 97:6–107:3 there is a Greek papyrus, a book from the 300s AD now split between the Chester Beatty Library in Dublin and the University of Michigan. Campbell Bonner published it in 1937. It is older than any Ethiopic copy by about a thousand years, though it has gaps. The Plain English Translation follows the Ge'ez, as the site's source text. This part has not compared the Greek verse by verse; where a Greek reading is given (as at 100:6), it is reported from Bonner's edition.

a: before the Holy Great One
p: The sinners' words are read aloud in the heavenly court, as in Daniel 7 and Revelation 20.
b: In Daniel 7:10 "the court sat, and the books were opened." In Revelation 20:12 the dead are judged "by what was written in the books." The Epistle stresses that nothing is lost: every sin is written down every day (98:7–8; 104:7). Here the Ge'ez order is "the Great and Holy One"; the Plain English Translation uses this site's usual "the Holy Great One" (see 92:2).

a: The memory they keep of you is evil
p: A hard line. It may mean that sea and land, which God made, keep a record of the sinners' evil.
b: Word for word: "Woe to you sinners, who are in the middle of the sea and on dry land, whose memory is evil against you." Charles kept it that way. The Plain English Translation takes "whose memory" as the memory kept by sea and land. That fits 100:10–11 and 104:8, where sun, moon, clouds and rain, day and night, all witness against the sinners. Others take it simply as "your memory will be evil."

a: We have become rich, truly rich
p: Very close to Jesus' parable of the rich fool, who plans to store his goods and enjoy life (Luke 12:16–21).
b: The rich speak for themselves in 97:8–9: they are rich, they have all they wanted, and they will now do what they planned with full storerooms. In Luke 12:16–21 a rich man says he will build bigger barns and tell himself to relax, eat, drink and be merry, and God calls him a fool. Hosea 12:8 and Revelation 3:17 also quote the boast "I am rich." The parallel was studied in detail by Nickelsburg; most see shared tradition.

a: the workers on our estates are as many as water
p: The Ge'ez says the plowmen of their houses are 'like water, many.' Charles moved the phrase to the storerooms.
b: Charles rearranged the lines so the storerooms are "full as with water." The Ge'ez puts "like water" with the workers: the rich have as many farmhands as there are drops of water. Large estates with hired and enslaved workers were growing in Judea in the Hellenistic period, which fits the setting of these woes.
orig: ወከመ ፡ ማይ ፡ ብዙኅ ፡ ሐረስተ ፡ አብያቲነ (wä-kämä may bəzuḫ ḥärästä ʾäbyatinä)

a: it will quickly fly up and leave you
p: Proverbs 23:5: riches sprout wings and fly off like an eagle.
b: The Ge'ez says wealth will quickly "go up" (yäʿärrəg) from them. Proverbs 23:5 says of riches, "It is sure to make itself wings / and take off like an eagle for the open sky." Jesus warns against storing up treasure on earth, where moth and rust destroy (Matthew 6:19–21), and James 5:2–3 says the rich man's gold has rusted.

a: I swear to you
p: From 98:1 Enoch begins to swear oaths. Jesus later teaches his followers not to swear at all.
b: The Epistle has a chain of oaths (98:1, 4, 6; 99:6; 103:1; 104:1). An oath makes a statement as certain as a court verdict. Ge'ez ʾəmməḥəl is "I swear." In Hebrews 6:13–17 God himself swears to make his promise sure. But Jesus says "Do not swear at all" (Matthew 5:34; compare James 5:12). Enoch's oaths are not everyday promises but prophetic guarantees.

a: You men will put on more jewelry than a woman
p: The rich men dress in more finery than women. Luxury clothing was a sign of status.
b: Purple dye was among the most expensive goods of the ancient world and was worn by kings and the very rich (Luke 16:19; Revelation 18:12). The writer mocks men who outdress women and young girls, a common taunt in the ancient world. The line "they will be poured out like water" means all of it, and perhaps the men themselves, will be spilled away.

a: sin was not sent upon the earth
t: Where sin comes from: Compared with the Bible
p: People made sin themselves. This agrees with James 1:13–15, but seems to differ from the Watchers story.
b: In the Book of the Watchers, sin spreads because angels taught forbidden things, and God says "write all sin" against Azazel (10:8). Here Enoch swears that sin was not sent down; people created it. Scholars read this as a correction, or as a balance: the Watchers spread evil, but every person is still responsible. The 66 books also hold both. Sin enters through human choice (Genesis 3; James 1:13–15), yet Satan tempts (Genesis 3:1; 1 John 3:8). Ethiopian Orthodox teachers read the two passages together, as the Bible's own two sides.

a: Barrenness was not given to a woman
p: Barrenness is an example in Enoch's oath. As a rule it would clash with Sarah, Rachel and Hannah, whose wombs God closed.
b: This is a hard verse. It is the third example in an oath built on comparisons (98:4): a mountain does not become a slave, and in the same way sin was not sent from above but made by people. Barrenness too was not "given" but comes from "what her own hands have done." So the line first illustrates 98:4. Some take "her own hands" as deliberate acts, such as ending a pregnancy (compare 99:5); this site has not found which scholars hold this, so it is only a reported reading. As a rule about childless women it would clash with the 66 books, where God closes and opens wombs (Genesis 30:2; 1 Samuel 1:5) and righteous women are barren (Luke 1:6–7; John 9:2–3). The Greek papyrus covers this verse but was not checked here, and no Ethiopian Orthodox comment on it was found in this site's sources. The verse names one cause of childlessness; it does not say every childless woman is to blame.

a: every sin is written down in heaven
p: Sins are recorded every day. Malachi 3:16 has a book of remembrance; Revelation 20:12 has books opened.
b: The sinners think no one sees (Psalm 10:11; Psalm 94:7). Enoch answers that heaven keeps a daily record. Malachi 3:16 has a scroll of remembrance for those who fear the LORD; Revelation 20:12 has books by which the dead are judged. Jesus says that every careless word will be accounted for (Matthew 12:36).

a: you know of no ransom
p: Wealth cannot buy a life back from death, as Psalm 49 says.
b: Psalm 49:7–8 says no one can pay God a ransom for another person's life, because "the price for their lives is too high." The rich cannot buy their way out of judgment (Zephaniah 1:18). Christians hear the contrast with Mark 10:45, where the Son of Man gives his life "as a ransom for many."

a: who do evil and eat blood
p: Eating blood is forbidden in Genesis 9 and Leviticus 17, and again in Acts 15.
b: God forbids Noah's descendants to eat meat with its blood (Genesis 9:4), and Leviticus 17:10–14 repeats it for Israel. The giants in 7:5 drink blood. The early church kept the rule for Gentile believers (Acts 15:20, 29). Here the charge may be literal, or may picture the rich "drinking the blood" of the poor by violence, as in Micah 3:2–3.

a: They will cut your throats and kill you
p: The righteous will execute the sinners. Readers differ on how to hear this.
b: Like 91:12 and 95:3, this verse gives the righteous a role in the judgment. Some scholars connect it with the Maccabean wars; others read it as a picture of God's justice in the end, carried out by his people as in Daniel 7:22. Jesus forbids his followers to take revenge (Matthew 5:38–44), and Paul says "vengeance is mine" belongs to God (Romans 12:19). The Ethiopian Orthodox Church reads such verses as God's judgment, not as permission for violence.

a: No grave will be dug for you
p: In the ancient world, to lie unburied was the worst disgrace.
b: Being left unburied was a curse in the Bible (Deuteronomy 28:26; Jeremiah 22:19, Jehoiakim's "burial of a donkey"; Jeremiah 16:4). The rich who once died "in honor" (103:6) are told they will lose even a grave.

a: Woe to you who write lying words
p: Who were the writers of lying words? Perhaps teachers whose books taught a different law.
b: This woe and 104:10–11 suggest a quarrel over books. The writer's group had Enoch's books; others wrote books the writer called lies. Scholars suggest rival teachers of the law, or Hellenistic wisdom writings, or teachers who denied judgment after death (102:6–8). It shows that in Judea in the 100s BC people argued over which writings to trust, a question about the canon long before there was a canon.

a: break the eternal law
p: The sinners break 'the eternal law.' Most take it as the Law of Moses.
b: The Epistle mentions Moses' law only in passing (93:6), but here the sinners twist "the words of uprightness" and break "the eternal law." Most scholars take this as the Torah, perhaps as the writer's group read it. Isaiah 24:5 says the earth's people "broke the eternal covenant." The Plain English Translation keeps "law" for śərʿät.

a: Lay them before the angels as a witness
p: The angels bring the prayers of the righteous before God. Tobit and Revelation share the idea.
b: In 9:1–3 and 15:2 the angels bring the cries of the earth before God. Tobit 12:12 has the angel Raphael bring Tobit's prayer before the Holy One. Revelation 8:3–4 has an angel offer the prayers of God's people with incense. The 66 books do not give angels the role of carrying every prayer; Christian churches differ on whether angels intercede.

a: They will throw away even the babies they are nursing
p: In terrible times parents abandon their babies. Compare Lamentations 4 and Jesus on the last days.
b: The words "those in need" may mean the destitute, driven by hunger, as in the sieges of Lamentations 4:3–10 and Deuteronomy 28:53–57. Isaiah 49:15 asks whether a mother can forget her nursing child. Jesus speaks of woe to nursing mothers in the last days (Mark 13:17). Some translators read "those who are pregnant" for "those in need." Others render the line about children slipping from their hands as women miscarrying or aborting (E. Isaac's 1983 English is often cited this way; this is a report, not checked here).

a: Some worship unclean spirits and demons
p: Revelation 9:20 lists demons and idols of gold, silver, stone and wood, very close to this verse.
b: The list here (stones, images of gold, silver, wood and clay, unclean spirits and demons) is close to Revelation 9:20: "worshiping demons and idols of gold, silver, bronze, stone, and wood." Both draw on Deuteronomy 32:17 and Psalm 106:37, where Israel sacrificed to demons, and on mocking lists of idols in Psalm 115:4–8 and Daniel 5:23. 1 Enoch 19:1 says the Watchers' spirits led people to sacrifice to demons. Paul says pagan sacrifices are offered to demons (1 Corinthians 10:20).

a: in their shrines
p: The Ge'ez says 'and in shrines.' Charles read a different word meaning 'not according to knowledge.'
b: Dillmann has wä-bä-mḥəramat, "and in sanctuaries, holy places"; the EOTC text has "and to shrines." Charles translated "not according to knowledge," which comes from a different reading in the Ethiopic manuscripts he used (his English of 1917 was made before the Greek papyrus was published); this site has not identified which manuscripts. The Plain English Translation follows the Ge'ez as printed.

a: by what they see in their dreams
p: Idol worship is tied to fear and false dreams. Deuteronomy 13 and Jeremiah 23 warn about lying dreamers.
b: Ancient people sought dreams at shrines and paid dream-interpreters. Deuteronomy 13:1–5 says a dreamer who leads people to other gods must not be followed, and Jeremiah 23:25–32 condemns prophets of lying dreams. Enoch's own visions (chapters 83–90) came in dreams too, so the difference is not the dream but the god behind it.

a: blessed are all who accept the words of wisdom
p: A blessing in the middle of the woes, like Psalm 1 and Jesus' beatitudes.
b: Blessings and woes stand side by side in Deuteronomy 27–28, in Luke 6:20–26 and here. "Blessed" (bəḍuʿ) matches the Hebrew ashre and the Greek makarios. The blessed accept wisdom, keep to the Most High's paths and "will be saved," which makes the woes a call to choose.

a: You will be killed in Sheol
p: Sheol is the world of the dead in the Hebrew Bible. In 1 Enoch it becomes a place where judgment begins.
b: Ge'ez siʾol is borrowed from the Hebrew she'ol. In most of the Hebrew Bible it is the dark place where all the dead go. In 1 Enoch 22 it has separate places for the righteous and the wicked, and the Epistle says the sinners will suffer there (99:11; 103:7–8). This is a step between the Old Testament's Sheol and the New Testament's Hades and Gehenna (Luke 16:23).

a: with the hard labor of others
p: Building with other people's toil: forced or unpaid labor, condemned by Jeremiah.
b: Kings and rich landowners used forced and unpaid labor for building (1 Kings 5:13; Jeremiah 22:13). The Law commanded fair and prompt wages (Leviticus 19:13; Deuteronomy 24:14–15), and James 5:4 says unpaid wages cry out against the rich.

a: the eternal inheritance of their fathers
p: The ancestral land and law. Selling out the ancestors' inheritance was a serious crime in Israel.
b: In Israel land was a family inheritance that was not supposed to be sold off forever (Leviticus 25:23; 1 Kings 21:3, where Naboth refuses to sell his vineyard). The "measure" may be the fair share of land, or the measure of the Law. Either way the sinners give up what their ancestors handed down and chase other gods.

a: fathers and their sons will be struck down together
p: In the last days families turn on each other, as in Micah 7 and Jesus' words in Mark 13.
b: The judgment begins with sinners killing one another. Micah 7:6 has a son despise his father; Ezekiel 38:21 and Zechariah 14:13 have enemies turn their swords on each other. Jesus says brother will betray brother and children rise against parents (Mark 13:12). 1 Enoch tells the giants' end the same way (10:9–12).

a: A horse will wade up to its chest in the blood of sinners
p: Revelation 14:20 has blood flow from the winepress 'as high as the horses' bridles.'
b: The picture of blood deep enough to reach a horse is close to Revelation 14:20, where blood flows as high as the horses' bridles for about 180 miles. Both are deliberate exaggerations of a total judgment. Many scholars think Revelation knew this image from Jewish tradition; later rabbinic texts use it for Rome's slaughter at Betar.

a: the angels will go down into the hiding places
p: Sinners try to hide from judgment; Amos 9 and Revelation 6 say there is no escape.
b: Amos 9:2–3 says that even if sinners dig into Sheol or hide on Mount Carmel, God will take them. In Revelation 6:15–17 the powerful hide in caves and call on the rocks to fall on them. The angels gather the sinners, as in Jesus' parables the angels gather the wicked out of the kingdom (Matthew 13:41, 49).

a: to guard them like the pupil of an eye
p: God sets angels over the righteous, guarding them like the pupil of an eye (Deuteronomy 32:10).
b: "The apple of his eye" in older English is the pupil: Deuteronomy 32:10 and Psalm 17:8 use it for those God guards with special care. Psalm 91:11 says God commands his angels to guard his people. Jesus says the little ones have angels who see the Father's face (Matthew 18:10). Here the angels guard the righteous until the end. The Ge'ez says "like the daughter of the eye."
orig: ከመ ብንተ ዐይን (kämä bəntä ʿayn), 'like the daughter of the eye'

a: Even if the righteous sleep a long sleep
p: The 'long sleep' is death, and the righteous need not fear it. Compare 1 Thessalonians 4.
b: Here sleep plainly means death, as in Daniel 12:2. The verse comforts those whose friends have died before seeing justice. Paul comforts the Thessalonians in the same way about believers who "have fallen asleep" (1 Thessalonians 4:13–17). Whether the dead are aware during the long sleep the Epistle does not say; 102:4–5 and 103:3–4 speak of their spirits as alive.

a: will see what is true
t: See the truth, or be safe?
p: The Ge'ez word can mean 'truth' or 'surely.' Charles read 'the wise in security.'
b: Dillmann has wä-ʾəmunä, from the root for "faithful, true" (the root of "amen"). It may mean the wise will "surely" see, or see "what is true." Charles translated "see the wise in security." The Plain English Translation follows the Ge'ez as best it can. Notice that the verse speaks of "this book": the writer expects his words to be read. The Greek papyrus here has "this letter," as Bonner notes in his introduction (1937); see the variant.

a: burn them with fire
p: The wicked burn the righteous with fire. This may reflect real executions in the writer's day.
b: This is one of the few places where the Epistle describes violence against the righteous in detail. Burning was used to punish and terrify. 2 Maccabees 7:3–5 tells of Jewish martyrs tortured over fire under Antiochus IV, and 2 Maccabees 6:11 tells of people burned in caves for keeping the Sabbath. Scholars are not sure the verse points to one event; it may be general. Hebrews 11:34 remembers those who "quenched the power of fire."

a: who lie awake to think up evil
p: Micah 2:1: woe to those who plan evil on their beds and carry it out at dawn.
b: The Ge'ez says they "keep watch" (tətäggähu), the same root as "Watchers" (təguhan): the sinners stay awake like the fallen angels, but for evil. Micah 2:1 cries woe to those who lie awake plotting and do it in the morning "since their hands are strong enough." Psalm 36:4 says the same of the wicked.

a: the angels will search out your deeds in heaven
p: Dillmann: the angels will search out the deeds. The EOTC text: God will ask the angels about them.
b: Dillmann's text makes the angels the investigators. The printed Ethiopian Bible reads that God "will inquire from the angels" about the deeds, as Charles translated. The sun, moon and stars are witnesses either way, because they see everything people do by day and night (104:8). See the variant.

a: He will call every cloud, mist, dew and rain to testify against you
p: Heaven and earth are witnesses in Deuteronomy, and the rain is held back as a sign of judgment.
b: Moses calls heaven and earth as witnesses against Israel (Deuteronomy 30:19; Deuteronomy 32:1). Deuteronomy 11:17 warns that God will shut the heavens so there is no rain, and Elijah's drought shows it happening (1 Kings 17:1; James 5:17). Rain was life in a land with no great river; refusing rain was the clearest sign that creation stood against the sinner.

a: give gifts to the rain
p: Sarcasm: the rich bribe judges, so let them try bribing the rain.
b: The rich are used to buying what they need, including verdicts. Enoch mocks them: go ahead and pay the rain and dew in gold and silver. The answer is obvious. Bribery is condemned in Exodus 23:8 and Deuteronomy 16:19; Isaiah 1:23 says the rulers love bribes.

a: all you children of heaven
p: An odd address to sinners. It may be a slip in the text, or a call to look up at heaven like its children.
b: Elsewhere the faithful are "children of righteousness" (105:2) and the guilty are "children of the earth" (100:6; 102:3). Here the sinners seem to be addressed as "children of heaven." Some think the text first read "children of men" or "children of the earth." Others take it as a reminder that all people were made by the God of heaven. The Plain English Translation keeps the Ge'ez.

a: the ship captains
p: The Ge'ez says 'kings of ships,' probably a translation of a Greek word for ship-owners or captains.
b: Nägäśtä ʾäḥmar means literally "kings of ships." It most likely renders a Greek term for the master of a ship. The sailors' fear of the sea is a classic picture: Psalm 107:23–30 describes sailors in a storm, their courage melting, until they cry to the LORD; Jonah 1:5 has sailors afraid and praying. Sailors fear the sea, but sinners do not fear the one who made it (101:9).

a: bound all of it with sand
p: God set sand as the sea's boundary (Jeremiah 5:22; Job 38).
b: Jeremiah 5:22 has God ask, "Is it me you do not fear? ... I made the sand a border for the sea." That is exactly the argument of chapter 101: fear the Creator who controls the sea. Job 38:8–11 and Psalm 104:9 also describe God fixing the sea's limits. In the ancient Near East the sea often stood for chaos, which only God can tame.

a: When he rebukes it, it is afraid and dries up
p: God's rebuke dries the sea, as at the Sea of Reeds (Psalm 106:9; Nahum 1:4).
b: "He scolded the Sea of Reeds, and it went dry" (Psalm 106:9). Nahum 1:4 and Isaiah 50:2 use the same picture: at God's rebuke the sea dries and its fish rot. Jesus rebukes the wind and waves and the disciples ask, "Who is this?" (Mark 4:39–41).

a: When he sends out his voice against you
p: The voice of the LORD shakes heaven and earth, as in Psalm 29 and Joel.
b: In Psalm 29 the voice of the LORD breaks cedars and shakes the wilderness. Joel 3:16 says the LORD roars from Zion and heaven and earth shake. Hebrews 12:26 recalls God's voice shaking the earth at Sinai and promises he will shake heaven too. Chapter 102 is the cosmic shaking that the woes have been warning about.

a: the Great Glory
p: A name for God on his throne, used in the Book of the Watchers (14:20).
b: "The Great Glory" (ʿäbiy səbḥat) is God seated in the heavenly temple in Enoch's throne vision (14:20). Even the angels try to hide from his face when he comes to judge. Compare Isaiah 2:10, "bury yourself in the dust, away from the dread of the LORD," and Revelation 6:16. The writer of Hebrews calls God "the Majesty on high" (Hebrews 1:3).

a: you souls of the righteous
p: Enoch now speaks to the righteous who have died. Their souls are alive and can hope.
b: From 102:4 to 104:8 the Epistle answers a bitter question: what about the righteous who suffered and died with no justice? Enoch addresses their souls directly. This assumes the soul lives on after death, an idea that grows in Jewish writings of this period (22:1–14; Wisdom of Solomon 3:1, "the souls of the righteous are in the hand of God"). Christians read it alongside Revelation 6:9–11, where the souls of the martyrs cry out and are told to rest a little longer.

a: Look instead to the day that belongs to the sinners
p: The Ge'ez here is hard. 'Look' is supplied to make a sentence: the day meant is the sinners' day of judgment.
b: Word for word the Ge'ez reads "but now, on the day in which you became sinners, and on the day of curse and punishment." That does not fit the comfort of the verse, and it may be damaged. The Plain English Translation supplies "Look" and reads the day as the one that belongs to the sinners: the day of their curse. Charles's "wait for the day of the judgement of sinners" gives the same sense. The Greek papyrus covers this verse, but this part has not checked its reading.
orig: በዕለት ፡ እንተ ፡ ባቲ ፡ ኮንክሙ ፡ ኃጥኣነ (bäʿlät ʾəntä bati konkəmu ḫaṭʾanä)

a: The righteous die just as we die
p: The sinners argue like Ecclesiastes: all die alike. Wisdom of Solomon answers them the way Enoch does.
b: The sinners' speech (102:6–8) uses ideas found in the Bible itself: "one fate comes to the righteous and to the wicked" (Ecclesiastes 9:2) and "who knows whether the spirit of human beings goes up above?" (Ecclesiastes 3:21). Wisdom of Solomon 2:1–5 puts a very similar speech in the mouth of the ungodly and answers it. Enoch's answer is that the end is different, even if death looks the same. Paul faces the same argument: "Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die" (1 Corinthians 15:32).
r: Ecclesiastes 3:19–21; Ecclesiastes 9:2–3; Wisdom of Solomon 2:1–5; 1 Corinthians 15:32

a: you are content to eat and drink
p: 'Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die' (Isaiah 22:13) is the sinners' creed.
b: The rich live only for this life: eating, drinking, robbing, getting rich, enjoying good days. Isaiah 22:13 quotes such people, and Paul repeats it (1 Corinthians 15:32). Jesus' story of the rich man and Lazarus begins with a man who "made merry in splendor every day" (Luke 16:19).

a: how their end was peace
t: The end of the upright is peace
p: Psalm 37:37: 'Watch the upright, for there is a future for the person of peace.'
b: Enoch asks the sinners to look at how the righteous die: in peace, without violence on their hands. Psalm 37:37 says to watch the blameless, for the man of peace has a future. Verse 11 may be Enoch's own sad description, or the sinners' reply: "yet they perished." The Ge'ez does not mark a speaker, so the Plain English Translation gives no quotation marks.

a: I know this mystery
p: Enoch knows heavenly 'mysteries': God's hidden plans, revealed to him and written in books.
b: Məśṭir is a borrowing of the Greek mystērion, through Aramaic raz. In Daniel 2:18–30 God reveals a raz to Daniel. The Dead Sea Scrolls speak of "the mystery of what is to be" (raz nihyeh). Paul uses the same word for God's plan revealed in Christ (Romans 16:25; Ephesians 3:3–6). The Epistle has several mysteries: the reward of the righteous here, and the fate of Enoch's books (104:10–12).

a: your share will be far greater than the share of the living
t: Reward after death: Compared with the Bible
p: A clear hope of reward after death for those who suffered unjustly. The later books of the Bible share it.
b: Much of the Hebrew Bible expects reward in this life (Deuteronomy 28; Psalm 37:25), though Job and some psalms protest. The Epistle states plainly that the righteous dead have a better share than the living. This agrees with Daniel 12:2–3 and with the New Testament (Luke 16:25; 2 Corinthians 4:17; Philippians 1:21–23). All churches accept this hope from the Bible; the Epistle is valued as early evidence of how Jews were already thinking before Christ.

a: Your spirits will live
p: The Ge'ez says the spirits of the righteous 'will rejoice and be glad.' Charles has 'shall not perish.'
b: The verse opens "and your spirits will live." Dillmann's Ge'ez then says "their spirits will rejoice and be glad." Charles's "their spirits shall not perish" comes from a different reading in the Ethiopic manuscripts he used (his English of 1917 was made before the Greek papyrus was published); this site has not identified which. The switch from "your" to "their" is in the Ge'ez.

a: How blessed are the sinners!
p: The friends of the rich call them blessed because they had long, easy lives. Psalm 73 struggles with the same sight.
b: Psalm 73:3–12 describes the psalmist's envy of the arrogant who have no struggles and die at ease. Job 21:13 says the wicked spend their days in prosperity and go down to Sheol in peace. Malachi 3:15 quotes people who call the arrogant blessed. Enoch's answer is the same as Psalm 73:17: understand their final end.

a: Into darkness and chains and burning flame
p: The punishment of sinners copies the punishment of the Watchers: darkness, chains, fire.
b: The fallen angels are bound in darkness and thrown into fire (10:4–6, 12–13). Now sinful people share their fate. Jude 6 and 2 Peter 2:4 speak of angels kept in chains under darkness. Jesus speaks of the outer darkness and the eternal fire made ready for the devil and his angels (Matthew 25:41).

a: Do not say about the righteous and good who are still alive
p: Verses 9–15 are a lament of the suffering righteous. Enoch quotes it to answer it in chapter 104.
b: Both Ge'ez texts have ʾitəbälwomu lä-ṣadqan: "do not say to them, to the righteous," or "about the righteous." The ending -omu on the verb points to the righteous as the ones spoken about or to, not as the ones addressed, so the Plain English Translation translates "do not say about." Some modern translators instead take the line as spoken to the righteous ("you righteous, do not say"); this site has not checked whether the Greek papyrus supports that. Either way, the words that follow are the complaint of the living righteous: they toiled, were robbed, became the tail instead of the head, and no ruler listened. Enoch quotes them honestly before answering them (104:1–6). It is one of the clearest pictures of the readers' real life.

a: We hoped to be the head, but we became the tail
p: Deuteronomy 28 promises the obedient will be the head, not the tail. The righteous feel the promise has been reversed.
b: In Deuteronomy 28:13 the LORD promises the obedient that they will be the head and not the tail; in Deuteronomy 28:44 the disobedient become the tail. The righteous kept the covenant and still got the curse. Their complaint is a sharp question to the Bible's own promise, which Enoch answers by pointing beyond death.

a: we complained about them to the rulers
p: The Ge'ez word usually means 'angels.' Here it most likely means the human authorities who ignored the poor.
b: Mälaʾəkt is the plural of mälʾak, "messenger, angel," but in Ge'ez it can also name chiefs and officials. The context points to people: these rulers helped the robbers and hid the murders (103:15). So most translators read "rulers." The same word comes back in 104:3, where all the distress "will be demanded from the rulers." Some read angels, since in 1 Enoch angels bring complaints to God.

a: They hide our murder
p: The authorities hid the killings. The poor had nowhere to turn for justice.
b: This is the bleakest line of the lament. Ecclesiastes 4:1 sees the tears of the oppressed with no one to comfort them, and power on the side of the oppressors. Isaiah 59:14–15 says justice is driven back. The readers had no court that would hear them, so Enoch moves their case to the court of heaven (104:1–3).

a: Your names are written before the glory of the Great One
p: Jesus tells his disciples to rejoice that their names are written in heaven (Luke 10:20).
b: Earthly records hid the murders of the poor (103:15), but heaven writes the names of the righteous. Daniel 12:1 speaks of those "written in the book"; Jesus says, "Be glad that your names stand written in heaven" (Luke 10:20); and Revelation has the book of life (Revelation 3:5). Compare the opposite in 108:3, where sinners' names are wiped out.

a: you will shine like the lights of heaven
t: Shining like the stars: Compared with the Bible
p: Daniel 12:3 and Matthew 13:43 say the same. Here the righteous become like the angels.
b: Daniel 12:3 says the wise will shine like the brightness of the sky and like the stars forever. Jesus says the righteous will shine like the sun in their Father's kingdom (Matthew 13:43). The Epistle adds that the righteous will be companions of the army of heaven (104:6) and joyful like the angels (104:4). Jesus says the raised "are like angels in the heavens" (Mark 12:25). The match is close; scholars debate whether Daniel or Enoch came first.

a: Keep crying out for judgment
p: Like the widow in Jesus' parable, the righteous are to keep crying for justice.
b: The lament said no one heard their cry (103:14). Now they are told to keep crying, because heaven hears. Jesus' parable of the widow and the unjust judge teaches the same: "Will God, then, not get justice for his chosen, who call out to him day and night?" (Luke 18:1–8).

a: you will be companions to the army of heaven
p: The righteous will join the angels, God's heavenly army.
b: The Ge'ez ḥara sämay means "the army of heaven," the angels (compare Luke 2:13, "a crowd of heaven's army"). Being "companions" (sutufan) of angels instead of sinners (97:4) is a striking hope. Hebrews 12:22 says believers have come "to angels by the tens of thousands."

a: do not praise your idols
p: The Ge'ez says 'do not praise your idols.' Charles has 'nor take account of your idols.'
b: ʾitäsäbbəḥəwwo means "do not praise." Charles's "take account of" seems to come from a different reading. Idols here may be literal, or may mean anything trusted in place of God, such as wealth (compare Colossians 3:5, greed "which is idolatry").

a: they will write books of their own words
t: Changing Enoch's words: Compared with the Bible
p: Enoch warns against people who change his words, like the warning at the end of Revelation.
b: Deuteronomy 4:2 forbids adding to or taking away from God's commands, and Revelation 22:18–19 warns anyone who adds to or removes from its prophecy. Enoch makes the same claim for his own books. Ethiopian Orthodox teachers point to this as the book's claim to be revealed. Other churches answer that a book's claim about itself does not settle whether it is Scripture; the church's long reception does, and outside Ethiopia the church did not receive 1 Enoch. Both sides agree that the warning shows the writer believed his book was sacred.

a: in their own languages
p: Enoch foresees his books written in other languages, and so they were: Aramaic, Greek, Ge'ez and more.
b: This verse seems to expect translation. The book was written in Aramaic (and perhaps partly Hebrew), translated into Greek, and from Greek into Ge'ez sometime between the 400s and 600s AD. Pieces survive in Latin, Coptic and Syriac too. Only in Ge'ez did the whole book survive, copied by the Ethiopian church, which kept it as Scripture. Ethiopian Orthodox readers see this verse fulfilled in their own tradition.

a: books will be given to the righteous and the wise
p: Enoch's own books, given to the righteous at the end. Ethiopian readers see their Bible here.
b: Most scholars think the writer means 1 Enoch itself, or the whole Enoch library, given to his community in the seventh week as "sevenfold teaching" (93:10). Daniel 12:4 has Daniel seal his book until the end. Ethiopian Orthodox readers take the verse as a promise fulfilled in the books of the church. Other Christians apply the hope of true books given to the faithful to the 66 books.

a: says the Lord
t: Missing in the Greek, present in the Aramaic
p: Chapter 105 is not in the Greek papyrus, but the Aramaic 4Q204, as Milik restores it, seems to have had it.
b: The Chester Beatty–Michigan papyrus has no chapter 105: chapter 106 follows 104 directly (Bonner, 1937). But the Aramaic copy 4Q204 (4QEnoch-c), made in the first century BC, seems to have had it. J. T. Milik (1976, pp. 220–222) places 105:1–2 in fragment 5, column i, lines 21–23, though most of the words there are his restorations. He concludes that the chapter was in the Aramaic and that the Greek copyist skipped it, his eye jumping between two similar endings (homoeoteleuton). So the chapter's absence from the Greek does not by itself show that it was added later. See the variants on 105:1–2.

a: I and my son
p: God speaks of 'my son.' Christians have heard the Father and the Son; scholars debate the phrase.
b: This is a rare phrase in Jewish writings. 4 Ezra 7:28 speaks of "my son the Messiah," and Psalm 2:7 has God call the king "my son." Christian readers, including Ethiopian Orthodox teachers, hear the Father and the Son joined with the faithful (John 14:23). J. T. Milik judged that the gap in the Aramaic 4Q204 at this line is too short for the first half of the verse, and so took "I and my son" as a Christian gloss added to a chapter that was otherwise in the Aramaic (1976, pp. 68, 222). That rests on measuring a damaged line; it is his reconstruction, not a preserved reading. Others read "my son" as Jewish usage for the Messiah or for Israel (Exodus 4:22).

a: Rejoice in truth
p: The Ge'ez bä-ʾäman means 'in truth.' Charles took it as 'Amen.'
b: Bäʾäman is "in truth, truly," from the same root as "amen." Charles ended the chapter with "Amen," which suits a closing. The Plain English Translation keeps "in truth."

a: my son Methuselah took a wife for his son Lamech
t: The birth of Noah: a story also told at Qumran
p: Chapters 106–107 retell Noah's birth. The Genesis Apocryphon from Qumran (1Q20) tells the same story in Aramaic.
b: Genesis 5:28–29 says only that Lamech fathered a son and named him Noah. Chapters 106–107 fill the gap with a story, told by Enoch in the first person. The same tale, longer, is in the Aramaic Genesis Apocryphon from Qumran Cave 1 (1Q20, columns 2–5): there Lamech suspects his wife Bitenosh of conceiving by a Watcher, she swears she has not, and Methuselah goes to Enoch. Pieces of these chapters in Aramaic also survive in 4Q204 (4QEnoch-c): Milik (1976) assigns fragment 5, column i to 104:13–106:2 and column ii to 106:13–107:2. A Latin excerpt of chapter 106 also survives in a British Library manuscript, found by M. R. James (1893) and mentioned by Bonner (1937). The Plain English Translation uses the name forms Lamech and Noah from Genesis.

a: white as snow and red as a rose in bloom
t: A baby who looks like an angel
p: White hair like wool and a face like the sun: the newborn Noah looks like the heavenly beings.
b: The details match descriptions of heavenly figures. Daniel 7:9 gives the Ancient of Days hair white like wool; Revelation 1:14 gives the risen Jesus hair white as wool and snow; angels' faces shine like the sun (Matthew 28:3; Revelation 10:1). No wonder Lamech fears the child is a Watcher's son. The story may also teach that Noah, the one righteous man, already shines with heaven's light, as Moses' face did (Exodus 34:29).
r: Daniel 7:9; Revelation 1:14; Matthew 17:2; Exodus 34:29; Song of Songs 5:10

a: spoke with the Lord of righteousness
p: The baby speaks and praises God at birth. Later stories told the same of other heroes.
b: Miracle births mark great figures in many traditions. Here the newborn speaks with God (106:3) or blesses him (106:11). The Greek papyrus and the Genesis Apocryphon tell the story too, with small differences. Readers have compared the birth of Moses, whom his mother saw was "beautiful" (Exodus 2:2), and the shining birth stories later told of Moses and of Jesus in Jewish and Christian legend. The Gospels do not tell such marvels of Jesus' infancy.

a: He looks like the children of the angels of heaven
p: Lamech fears the child is a half-angel, like the giants born to the Watchers.
b: The fear only makes sense because of Genesis 6:1–4, where "the sons of God" took human wives, and because of 1 Enoch's story of the Watchers fathering giants (6:1–7:6). Lamech worries that his wife has been with an angel. Charles's English here says "the sons of the God of heaven"; Dillmann's Ge'ez says "the children of the angels of heaven." Enoch's answer will be that the child is truly Lamech's (106:18).

a: he lives among the angels
p: Genesis says God took Enoch. 1 Enoch says he now lives with the angels at the ends of the earth.
b: Genesis 5:24 says Enoch "was gone, for God took him." Hebrews 11:5 says he was taken so that he did not see death. The Enoch books place him with the angels (12:1–2) and here "at the ends of the earth" (106:8), where the living can still reach him by calling out. Jubilees 4:23 puts him in the Garden of Eden, writing down the judgment of the world.

a: he came to me at the ends of the earth
p: Enoch suddenly tells the story in the first person: 'he came to me.'
b: Verses 1–7 sounded like a narrator. Now Enoch says "me," so the whole birth story is Enoch's own account, written for Methuselah. This fits the Epistle, which is all Enoch's voice. In the Genesis Apocryphon, Lamech tells the story in the first person instead.

a: In the generation of my father Jared
p: The Watchers came down in the days of Jared, whose name sounds like the Hebrew 'to come down.'
b: 1 Enoch 6:6 says the Watchers came down "in the days of Jared" on Mount Hermon. The name Jared (Yered, Genesis 5:15–20) sounds like the Hebrew yarad, "to come down," and Jubilees 4:15 makes the same connection. The Ge'ez "some from the heights of heaven" is how the Plain English Translation renders a short phrase that names no subject; it means the Watchers. Here the Ethiopian Church's printed text reads betä wäldu, "the house of his son," where Dillmann has bätwəldu, "in the generation of"; the Plain English Translation follows Dillmann, which matches 6:6.

a: They have married some of them and fathered children by them
t: The sons of God: Compared with the Bible
p: Enoch reads Genesis 6:1–4 as angels marrying women. Many Christians and Jews read it differently.
b: Genesis 6:1–4 says "the sons of God" took wives from "the daughters of humankind." 1 Enoch reads the sons of God as angels, as most Jewish readers did before Jesus and as many church fathers did (Justin, Irenaeus, Tertullian). Jude 6–7 and 2 Peter 2:4 may echo this reading. From the 200s (Julius Africanus), and widely after Augustine, many Christians read them instead as the line of Seth. Jewish teachers came to read them as nobles or judges and rejected the angel reading (Genesis Rabbah 26:5; Targum Onkelos; Rashi). Most Ethiopian Orthodox teachers follow Enoch's reading. Other churches allow both; Jesus' saying that angels do not marry (Mark 12:25) is often cited against it.

a: great destruction for one year
p: Genesis dates the Flood from the 600th year of Noah, second month, to the next year: about a year.
b: Genesis 7:11 dates the start of the Flood and Genesis 8:14 the drying of the earth a little more than a year later. The Ge'ez phrase "water of the flood" (mayä ʾayḫ) is the Ge'ez Bible's name for the Flood.
orig: ማየ አይኅ (mayä ʾayḫ), 'water of the flood'

a: his three sons will be saved with him
p: The Ge'ez says 'his three children.' The Plain English Translation says 'sons,' following Genesis: Shem, Ham and Japheth.
b: Ge'ez däqiq means "children"; the numeral three makes clear that Shem, Ham and Japheth are meant (Genesis 6:10). Their wives were saved too (Genesis 7:13; 1 Peter 3:20, eight people in all).

a: beings on the earth who are not of spirit but of flesh
p: The Ge'ez word before 'not of spirit' is unclear. Charles read 'giants'; the Plain English Translation says 'beings.' See the variant.
b: Both Ge'ez texts have ʾəllä yarbəḥ before "not of spirit," words that do not give clear sense and are probably corrupt. Charles translated "giants," as in 7:2 and 15:8; "beings" in the Plain English Translation is also a supplied word, chosen because it adds the least. The Aramaic 4Q204 covers this verse (fragment 5, column ii): J. T. Milik's English (1976, p. 224) has the offspring as creatures "of flesh" rather than spiritual beings, which agrees with the sense here. The Greek papyrus also covers the verse, but this part has not checked its reading. The verb is future ("they will father"): Enoch speaks of the Watchers' offspring still to come before the Flood, after their first children (106:14). The giants were born of spirit (angels) and flesh (women); 15:8–10 says that when they die their spirits become evil spirits on the earth.

a: Name him Noah, for he will be left to you as a remnant
p: Genesis explains Noah's name as 'relief' or 'comfort.' Here he is a 'remnant,' and in 107:3 one who brings joy.
b: In Genesis 5:29 Lamech names him Noah saying, "This one will bring us relief" (Hebrew yenachamenu, "comfort us," a play on Noach). 1 Enoch gives two explanations: he will be a remnant (täräf, the one left over, 106:18) and he will make the earth glad (107:3). The idea of the remnant ties Noah to the faithful few of the Epistle's own day (93:10).

a: even more injustice than what was done on the earth before
p: The Flood does not end sin. Evil returns, worse than before, until the final generation of righteousness.
b: This matches the pattern of 91:5–7 and 93:4: after the Flood, injustice grows again. Genesis itself says the human heart is still evil after the Flood (Genesis 8:21). Christians read this pattern as showing that judgment alone cannot cure sin; Ethiopian Orthodox teachers have read the "generation of righteousness" (107:1) as pointing to Christ and his church. Most scholars read it as the writer's own hope for his community.

a: until a generation of righteousness arises
p: Sin will go on until a generation of righteousness arises: the same hope as the Ten Weeks.
b: This joins the Noah story to the Epistle's main hope. The writer's readers are the righteous generation of the seventh week (93:10), and the Flood story is told to show that God saves a righteous remnant through judgment. Psalm 14:5 says "God stands with the circle of the righteous," where the Hebrew word for "circle" (dor) also means "generation." Jesus compares his own generation to Noah's (Luke 17:26–27).

a: he will bring joy to the earth after all the destruction
p: Genesis 5:29: 'This one will bring us relief.' The Ge'ez says he will make the earth glad.
b: Lamech's naming words in Genesis 5:29 are "This one will bring us relief from our work and from the painful labor of our hands." The Ge'ez verb yastäfeśśəḥa means "make glad, console."
