Here the relief is for the whole earth, after the Flood washes it clean. Many readers see Noah as a picture of a savior who brings rest after judgment (Hebrews 11:7; 1 Peter 3:20–21).

a: He named that child Noah
t: The end of the Greek copy
p: The Greek papyrus ends here, with the title 'Epistle of Enoch.' Chapter 108 is not in the Greek or the Aramaic.
b: The Chester Beatty–Michigan papyrus stops at 107:3 and writes the title Epistle of Enoch under it (Bonner, 1937). No Aramaic fragment of chapter 108 has been found. So the oldest copies of 1 Enoch seem to have ended here. Chapter 108 is found only in Ge'ez.

a: Another book that Enoch wrote
p: Chapter 108 calls itself 'another book.' Scholars think it was added later, perhaps in the first century AD.
b: The heading itself says this is a separate book. It is not in the Greek papyrus or among the Dead Sea Scrolls. Its ideas of a fiery place of chaos, of ascetics who gave their bodies to torment, and of "the generation of light" fit Jewish (or possibly Christian) circles around the time of the New Testament. Dates proposed run from the first century BC to the first century AD or later. It sums up 1 Enoch's themes as a closing word.

a: keep the law in the last days
p: The book is for those who keep the law in the last days.
b: Śərʿat here, as in 99:2, means God's law. "The last days" is the time the writer thinks he lives in (compare Isaiah 2:2; Daniel 10:14; Hebrews 1:2). Revelation describes the faithful as those who "keep the commandments of God and hold on to the testimony of Jesus" (Revelation 12:17).

a: their names will be wiped out of the holy books
p: Being wiped out of the book is the Bible's picture of final loss (Exodus 32:33; Psalm 69:28).
b: Moses asks to be blotted out of God's book, and God answers that he will blot out those who sin against him (Exodus 32:32–33). Psalm 69:28 prays that enemies be blotted out of the book of the living. Jesus promises the one who overcomes that he will never blot out his name (Revelation 3:5). Charles's English adds "the book of life"; Dillmann's Ge'ez has "the books of the holy ones."

a: a shapeless wilderness
t: A place that cannot be seen
p: The Ge'ez says a desert 'that cannot be seen': chaos before creation, as the Greek Genesis says of the earth.
b: Word for word the place is "a desert that does not appear" or "cannot be seen." The Greek translation of Genesis 1:2 says the earth was aoratos, "invisible," where the Hebrew has tohu, "formless." The place of punishment is uncreated chaos, "for there is no earth there." Compare 18:12 and 21:1–2, where Enoch sees a place that has no heaven above and no earth below.

a: the sound of crying and weeping, wailing and fierce pain
t: A place of fire: Compared with the Bible
p: A fiery place of punishment for the spirits of sinners. The New Testament speaks of Gehenna and the lake of fire.
b: The Hebrew Bible says little about punishment after death; Isaiah 66:24 and Daniel 12:2 are the clearest. 1 Enoch describes it often (10:13; 21:7–10; 27:2; 90:26). Jesus speaks of Gehenna, unquenchable fire and "weeping and grinding of teeth" (Mark 9:43–48; Matthew 13:42), and Revelation of the lake of fire (Revelation 20:14–15). So the picture agrees with the New Testament in outline. Churches differ on how literally to read such images, and on whether punishment is everlasting or ends in destruction.

a: those who twist everything that God has spoken through the mouth of the prophets
p: Those who distort the prophets are judged. 2 Peter 3:16 warns of people who twist the Scriptures.
b: This is one of two places in this part where the Ge'ez uses ʾƎgziʾabḥer (95:3; 108:6); here it comes with "the mouth of the prophets," a phrase common in the Bible (Luke 1:70; Acts 3:18, 21). The writer assumes a known body of prophetic books. 2 Peter 3:16 warns that ignorant people twist Paul's letters "as they also twist the other Scriptures." The EOTC text reads "his prophets."

a: those who made their bodies suffer
p: A new group: people who chose a hard life, scorned riches and suffered for God.
b: Verses 7–10 praise people who "made their bodies suffer," loved neither gold nor silver, did not long for earthly food, and gave their bodies to torment. This sounds like fasting and self-denial, and perhaps martyrdom. Such ideals were strong among some Jewish groups of the first century (Philo describes the Therapeutae) and among early Christian ascetics, which is one reason scholars debate whether chapter 108 is Jewish or Christian. Hebrews 11:35–38 praises the faithful who were tortured and went about poor.

a: They thought of themselves as a breath that passes away
p: Life as a breath: Psalm 39 and Psalm 144, and James 4:14.
b: "Every human being, even standing firm, is nothing but a puff of air" (Psalm 39:5); "A human is like a puff of air; his days are a shadow that slips past" (Psalm 144:4). James 4:14 says life is a mist that appears and vanishes. The humble lived as if they already knew this. "The Lord tested them" echoes Psalm 66:10 and 1 Peter 1:6–7, where faith is tested like gold.

a: yet they kept blessing me
p: The angel's speech suddenly becomes God's own voice: 'they blessed me,' 'I will call,' 'my holy name.'
b: From 108:10 to 108:12 the speaker says "me," "I will call," "my holy name." Only God can say this, so either the angel quotes God without warning, or the text has merged two speeches. Prophets do this often: the prophet's voice slides into God's (Isaiah 5:1–3; Jeremiah 8:18–9:3). The Plain English Translation keeps the Ge'ez as it is.

a: the generation of light
p: The good belong to 'the generation of light'; others are 'born in darkness.' The Scrolls and the New Testament share this language.
b: The Dead Sea Scrolls divide humanity into "the sons of light" and "the sons of darkness" (Community Rule 1:9–10; the War Scroll). Jesus speaks of "the children of light" (Luke 16:8; John 12:36), and Paul says "you are all children of light" (1 Thessalonians 5:5; Ephesians 5:8). Here God will even "transform those who were born in darkness" if they were faithful but unrewarded, which some read as saying that birth is not destiny. Others point to 108:14, where those born in darkness are led into darkness, and take the transformed ones as a narrower group: the faithful who were born in darkness but suffered without reward.

a: I will seat each one on his throne of honor
p: The faithful sit on thrones, as Jesus promises the Twelve and Revelation promises the victors.
b: Jesus tells the Twelve they will sit on twelve thrones (Matthew 19:28). Revelation 3:21 promises the one who overcomes a seat with Christ on his throne, and Revelation 20:4 shows thrones for the martyrs. Daniel 7:9 has "thrones" set up, plural. Here each faithful sufferer gets a throne of honor in shining light.

a: To the faithful he will give faithfulness
p: The Ge'ez plays on one word: to the faithful he gives faithfulness.
b: Lä-mähaymənan haymanotä uses one root (haymanot, faith) twice. In Ge'ez haymanot means both faith and faithfulness; it is the word the Ethiopian church uses for its creed. Compare Habakkuk 2:4 (the righteous will live by faithfulness) and Revelation 2:10 (be faithful to death).

a: where days and times have been written down for them
p: 1 Enoch ends with the righteous shining and the sinners going to their appointed place.
b: The book ends as it began: the righteous shine and the sinners meet their fixed end (compare 1:1, 8–9). Days and times written down for them recall the calendar of heaven in the Astronomical Book and the fixed weeks of history. For the Ethiopian Orthodox Church, this is the close of a book of Scripture read in its worship. For most other Christians, it is the close of an ancient Jewish book that shows the hopes the New Testament shares, which they test against the 66 books.
